title: The month-end close, step by step
seo_title: Month-end close in 6 steps: a checklist for small businesses
description: Catching up on the books once a year, at tax time, isn't bookkeeping. A proper month-end close has six steps: bank feeds, categorizing, reconciliations, accruals, amortization and P&L analysis.
body: Many small businesses keep their books once a year: a pile of receipts and statements handed to the accountant in time for the tax return. That isn't bookkeeping. It's a tax-season rush, and it leaves you running the business for eleven months on numbers that are out of date.
A proper month-end close has six steps. Most businesses that catch up once a year are only doing the first one.
## Step 1: Bank feeds

Connect every bank account and every card to your accounting system, so no transaction goes missing. An account that isn't connected only shows up when someone remembers to upload a statement, which is usually too late to be useful.
## Step 2: Categorize

Code every transaction the same way, every month. Payroll is payroll. Software is software. When the same expense lands in a different account from one month to the next, month-to-month comparisons stop meaning anything.
## Step 3: Reconciliations

Reconciliations prove the books are right. Bank accounts, cards and loans must match the books to the cent. Any difference gets investigated and explained before the month is closed, not a year later when nobody remembers what happened.
## Step 4: Accruals

Some bills haven't arrived by the time the month ends. Accruals record expenses and revenue in the month they actually happened, not when the invoice shows up. Without them, one month looks better than it was and the next looks worse.
## Step 5: Amortization
A year of insurance or software paid upfront is spread across the twelve months it covers. Otherwise one month carries a large expense and the other eleven look cheaper than they really are.
## Step 6: P&L analysis
The result of the close: reports ready by day 10 of the following month, compared with the previous month and with budget, with a clear note of what moved and why.
## A cycle, not a one-off
Once the six steps are in place, decisions are made on this month's numbers, not last year's. Then the close starts again the next month, in the same order.
A quick checklist:
- **Bank feeds:** every account and card connected.
- **Categorize:** the same coding every month.
- **Reconciliations:** bank, cards and loans match to the cent.
- **Accruals:** costs and revenue in the month they happened.
- **Amortization:** large upfront payments spread over the months they cover.
- **P&L analysis:** reports by day 10, against last month and budget.

title: Why your Sage Intacct reports disagree
seo_title: Sage Intacct dimension sprawl: why reports disagree and 5 steps to fix it
description: When Sage Intacct reports tell different stories, the cause is usually dimension sprawl: missing departments, duplicate locations and untagged lines. Five steps fix it for good.
body: The P&L shows one figure, the location report shows another, and the board pack shows a third. In Sage Intacct, this is rarely a calculation problem. It's usually dimension sprawl.

Dimension sprawl means missing departments, duplicate locations and transaction lines that were never tagged. Each report slices the same transactions differently, so each tells a slightly different story.
The underlying numbers are usually fine. What's missing is consistent tagging. Five steps fix it, so every report tells the same story.
## Step 1: Map your dimensions
Agree what each dimension value means, and retire duplicates nobody uses. If "NYC", "New York" and "NY Office" all exist as locations, keep one and merge the rest.
## Step 2: Make them required
Set bills, invoices and journals so they can't post without a department and a location. Requiring dimensions at entry stops new gaps from opening.
## Step 3: Clean up the history, once
Existing untagged lines still need fixing. Tag every line for the year and reclass anything posted to the wrong place. It's a one-time job, and Step 2 keeps it from piling up again.
## Step 4: Report by dimension
Build the P&L, the location view and the board pack on the same tags. When every report reads from the same dimensions, they can't drift apart.
## Step 5: Add a close check
Add one rule to the month-end close: untagged lines must be zero before the month is closed. This keeps the sprawl from coming back.
## In short
Tag it once, check it every month, and every report agrees.

title: Why your Shopify payout doesn't match your sales
seo_title: Why your Shopify payout doesn't match your sales (and how to reconcile it)
description: Shopify and Amazon payouts never match sales because fees, refunds and reserves come out first. Five steps, from a clearing account to A2X, make every dollar tie out.
body: Say a store sells $10,000 in a week. The payout that lands in the bank is smaller, and the two never seem to line up. It's one of the most common problems I see in eCommerce books.
The reason: fees, refunds and reserves are taken out before the payout reaches the bank. Nothing is missing. The money simply arrives in pieces. Five steps make every dollar tie out.
## Step 1: Split every payout
A payout isn't one number. Break each one into sales, discounts, refunds, fees and reserves, each on its own line. Once it's split, the difference between sales and deposit is fully explained.
## Step 2: Use a clearing account
Book sales to a clearing account rather than straight to the bank. Each payout then clears that account. Anything left over is a real difference worth investigating, not noise.
## Step 3: Automate with A2X
Splitting payouts by hand doesn't scale, especially across Shopify and Amazon. A2X posts one summary per payout, per channel, already mapped to the right accounts.
## Step 4: Match cost of goods to sales
Book cost of goods in the same month as the sale, so the margin is real. Sales in one month with the product cost in another make both months wrong.
## Step 5: Reconcile
At month end, every payout should match a bank deposit, and the clearing account should sit at zero. That's the proof the books are right.
## In short
Split every payout, automate the posting, and every month ties out.
